rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All three Qur'anic references to Jonah's great fish use the definite article, perhaps because the familiar legend makes the allegory self-explanatory.
rows.anchor: it carries the definite article al. This may possibly be due to the fact that the legend of Jonah was and is so widely known

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish's interior symbolizes Jonah's spiritual distress at fleeing his prophetic mission and the presence of God.
rows.anchor: symbolizes the deep darkness of spiritual distress of which 21:87 speaks: the distress at having "fled like a runaway slave" from his prophetic mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because humans are created weak, even prophets remain susceptible to human failings.
rows.anchor: since "man has been created weak" (4:28), even prophets are not immune against all the failings inherent in human nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah's being among those who glorify God means remembering God and repenting; his story has universal purport.
rows.anchor: I.e., to remember God and to repent: see 21:87, which reveals in its very formulation the universal purport of Jonah's story.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here taghut refers to seductive evil ambitions such as power-seeking, exploitative wealth, or immoral advancement, which disorient people and enslave them to passion.
rows.anchor: this term apparently circumscribes the seductive force of certain evil ambitions or desires - like striving after power for its own sake

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad cross-references the glad tidings to 10:62–64.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the verse as praising reasoned scrutiny of religious propositions, acceptance of what reason validates, and rejection of what fails its test.
rows.anchor: According to Razi, this describes people who examine every religious proposition (in the widest sense of this term) in the light of their own reason

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari advances a similar reading of reasoned examination, though in simpler terms.
rows.anchor: A somewhat similar view is advanced, albeit in simpler terms, by Tabari.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nature's repeated transformations and life-death cycle demonstrate God's might, especially His power to resurrect the dead.
rows.anchor: the above Qur'anic reference to the endless transformations and the miraculous cycle of life and death in all nature serves to emphasize God's almightiness and, specifically, His power to resurrect the dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The natural cycle indirectly recalls the preceding verse's assurance that God never fails to fulfil His promise.
rows.anchor: thus alluding, indirectly, to the statement at the end of the preceding verse that "never does God fail to fulfil His promise".

words: حِينَ مَوْتِهَا وَٱلَّتِى لَمْ تَمُتْ فِى مَنَامِهَا
rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi allegorically compares guidance to life and straying to death; temporary straying is like deathlike sleep followed by awakening.
rows.anchor: According to Razi, this passage connects allegorically with the preceding - the light of guidance being likened to life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beyond the allegory, the verse affirms God's might and exclusive power to create and withdraw life.
rows.anchor: of God's almightiness, and especially of His exclusive power to create and to withdraw life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yatawaffa literally means taking something away fully; tropically it means causing death, dying, or death because vital impulses are wholly withdrawn.
rows.anchor: the operative verb yatawaffa; it primarily denotes "He takes [something] away in full"; and because death is characterized

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep is traditionally likened to death because consciousness is absent in both, temporarily and partially in sleep, permanently in death.
rows.anchor: The traditional likening of sleep to death is due to the fact that in both cases the body appears to be devoid of consciousness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects translating anfus as souls here: the soul survives bodily death, so anfus means human beings.
rows.anchor: The popular translation of anfus - p1. of nafs - as "souls" is certainly inappropriate in the above context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his note on the opening words of 39:10.
rows.anchor: See note 16 on the opening words of verse 10 of this surah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's forgiveness of all sins is promised when sinners repent and turn to Him; 6:54 and 4:110 provide parallels of repentance and seeking forgiveness.
rows.anchor: Sc., "whenever the sinner repents and turns to Him": cf., for instance, 6:54

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unless context indicates otherwise, nafs means a human being; Asad therefore renders its associated pronouns as masculine despite the noun's feminine Arabic gender.
rows.anchor: it signifies a "human being"; hence, the personal pronouns relating to this term (which is feminine in Arabic) are masculine in my rendering.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to parallels concerning regret and wishing for another chance.
rows.anchor: Cf. 2:167 and 26:102, as well as 6:27-28 and the corresponding note 19.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad cross-references the promise to answer prayer with 2:186.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although earth's revival often symbolizes bodily resurrection, here it illustrates God's power to give spiritual life to hearts closed to His existence and omnipotence.
rows.anchor: it appears to be an illustration of God's power to bestow spiritual life upon hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse calls believers not to abandon hope that those denying truth may one day understand the Qur'anic message.
rows.anchor: call to the believer never to abandon the hope that "those who deny the truth" may one day grasp the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here din means religion's ethical and spiritual core, or faith generally, rather than religion including laws, which differed across dispensations.
rows.anchor: the term din cannot apply in this context to "religion" in its widest connotation, including religious laws

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse returns to the unchanging spiritual and moral principles underlying all revealed religions.
rows.anchor: the unchanging sameness of the spiritual and moral principles underlying all revealed religions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording implies that Muhammad learned what God had enjoined on Noah only through revelation.
rows.anchor: Lit., "which We have revealed unto thee", implying that it was only through revelation that the Prophet Muhammad came to know

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the command to uphold faith with statements that self-surrender to God is the only true religion.
rows.anchor: Cf. 3:19 - "the only [true) religion in the sight of God is [man's) self-surrender unto Him"; and 3:85

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command against division parallels the declarations that believers are one community under one Sustainer.
rows.anchor: Parallel with this principle, enunciated by all of God's apostles, is the categorical statement in 21:92 and 23:52

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari, Razi, Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Major commentators understand the verse as affirming ecumenical unity among monotheistic religions despite time-bound differences in their laws and practices.
rows.anchor: Most of the great commentators (e.g., Zamakhshari, Razi, Ibn Kathir) understand this as an unequivocal reference to the ecumenical unity of all religions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad cross-references the earth made as a cradle to 20:53.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form nazzala indicates recurrence, hence Asad's rendering 'again and again'.
rows.anchor: The grammatical form nazzala implies here recurrence: hence, "again and again".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad gives the literal sense of azwaj as 'all pairs'.
rows.anchor: Lit., "all pairs". Some commentators regard the term azwaj as synonymous

rows.speaker: Baghawi, Zamakhsharl, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: These commentators understand azwaj as kinds of things, beings, and phenomena.
rows.anchor: Some commentators regard the term azwaj as synonymous in this context with "kinds" (Baghawi, Zamakhsharl, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir)

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari reads the phrase as referring to polarity evident throughout creation.
rows.anchor: Others (e.g., Tabari) see in it a reference to the polarity evident in all creation.

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, as quoted by Razi, takes the phrase to denote opposites generally, such as sweet and sour or male and female.
rows.anchor: Ibn 'Abbas (as quoted by Razi) says that it denotes the concept of opposites in general

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi expands the idea to complementary pairs throughout creation, while God alone has no opposite, likeness, or complement.
rows.anchor: to which Razi adds that everything in creation has its complement, "like high and low, right and left, front and back

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects this account of pairs to the statement that nothing is comparable to God.
rows.anchor: Hence, the above sentence is an echo of the statement that "there is nothing that could be compared with Him" (112:4).

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators take 'their backs' to refer to the backs of both animals and ships; the singular pronoun refers collectively to all conveyances people use.
rows.anchor: according to all classical commentators, the "backs" of the above- mentioned animals and ships alike

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders istawa as gaining mastery, a connotation supported by Jawhari, Raghib, Lisan al-'Arab, and Lane.
rows.anchor: the verb istawa (lit., "he established himself") has often the connotation adopted by me: see Jawhari, Raghib and Lisan al-'Arab

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to note 147 on 11:116 for his rendering of mutraf, derived from tarafa.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of the term mutraf (derived from the verb tarafa), see note 147 on 11:116.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi argues that the passage refutes blind adoption of religious opinions: deniers followed their forebears without reason or clear revealed authority, and God condemns this.
rows.anchor: Commenting on this passage, Razi says: "Had there been in the Qur'an nothing but these verses, they would have sufficed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders dhikr here as 'a source of eminence'.
rows.anchor: For the above rendering of dhikr as "[a source of] eminence", see first half of note 13 on 21:10.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day, prophets are metaphorically asked what response their people gave to their message.
rows.anchor: The meaning is that on the Day of Judgment all prophets will be asked, metaphorically, as to what response they received from their people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Followers will answer for the spiritual and social use they made of revelation; Muhammad's community's promised eminence depends on conduct, not professed faith alone.
rows.anchor: those who professed to follow them will be called to account for the spiritual and social use they made
